Chapter 18
Troubleshooting IP, IPv6, and VLANs

This manual replaces Chapter 18 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (2020), book pages 495 to 548. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objectives, and marks every place where this document differs from the book. Chapter 18 is a troubleshooting chapter: it tests whether you can find a fault step by step, so the labs and the troubleshooting tables matter more than usual.

Read it top to bottom: pre-check, sections 18.1 to 18.6, the chapter-wide troubleshooting table, labs, review questions, then the revision sheet and tracker table. Nothing here was run on real Cisco equipment. Where a command or output was not run, it is marked CHECK .

Verification note. All address maths (the book's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, EUI-64 interface IDs, solicited-node multicast addresses, multicast MAC addresses, my lab addressing and the review answers) was calculated with a Python ipaddress script run in this session. It found that several of the book's IPv6 sample outputs do not agree with each other. These are listed in 18.5 and in the Changes and Gaps Log.
What was not done: no command in this document was run on a Cisco switch, router, simulator or client OS. Packet Tracer and real devices can differ from what is written here.

The idea in plain words. An endpoint is anything that connects to the network by wire or wireless and uses it. Most vendors charge by the number of active endpoints. Knowing the endpoint types matters because each one is connected a little differently, and that changes how you troubleshoot it. BOOK
| Endpoint | What the book says | Troubleshooting angle |

| 18.1.1 Desktops/Laptops | The most common endpoint. Most are Windows 10 or moving to it from Windows 7. Some Macs. Linux is rarely on the end-user side. All can use wired or wireless. | Check IP configuration first (18.3). Wired and wireless adapters each have their own settings. |

| 18.1.2 Mobile Phones/Tablets | Usually connect to an SSID. Companies often allow personal devices, restricted by security policy. iPhone, iPad, Android. Wireless only. | Wireless security settings and SSID. Often limited by policy. |

| 18.1.3 Access Points | They give wireless access to endpoints but are endpoints themselves. Usually wired for power and network. Wireless backhaul is possible in advanced designs. | Switch port VLAN and PoE. In v2.0 this is 2.2.b. |
| 18.1.4 IP Phones | VoIP. Phones use many switch ports, so PCs plug into the phone's built-in switch. Phones usually get power over Ethernet. | Voice VLAN and PoE on the switch port (Chapter 8). |
| 18.1.5 Internet of Things | Light bulbs, fridges, alarm systems and more are on the network and are endpoints. | Often static or DHCP addresses in a dedicated VLAN. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Dated operating system statements. The book says most companies are on Windows 10 or upgrading from Windows 7. Windows 7 left support in January 2020 (general knowledge). Windows 10 reached end of support on 14 October 2025, so as of today (15 October 2026) it is out of support unless the device has paid extended updates. Windows 11 is the supported Windows desktop. Status: secondary sources (university IT notices). The exam does not test the OS version, only the IP tools. UPDATED CHECK
Quick check 18.1
Q1. Why is an access point also called an endpoint?
Answer: It connects to the network (usually by wire) like any other device, even though it provides wireless access to others - vendors count it as an endpoint.
Q2. Why do office PCs often plug into the IP phone instead of the wall?
Answer: To save cabling and switch ports. The phone has a built-in switch - this is why the switch port carries a data VLAN and a voice VLAN.
Q3. Which endpoint types use wireless only, according to the book?
Answer: Mobile phones and tablets - desktops and laptops can use either.
Book pp. 497 to 498. Tracker rows: 18.2, 18.2.1. v2.0 relates to 1.7 (DHCP), 4.1 (AAA), 4.4 (DNS).
The idea in plain words. A server is a higher-end computer that provides infrastructure or application services to users. It comes in three forms. BOOK
| Form | What it is |
| Tower | A standard computer tower with a bit more resource than a normal PC. |
| Rack server | The most common type. Mounted in a rack, usually 1 rack unit (RU) high. Sometimes called a pizza box. |
| Blade server | The most complex. A blade that plugs into a large chassis. Designed to be very redundant and resilient. |
18.2.1 Server Roles
| Role | What it does (book p. 498) |
| Active Directory | Windows Server role for user and computer management. |
| DNS | Turns names into IP addresses. Without it we would need to memorise IP addresses. |
| DHCP | Gives endpoints their IP address dynamically. |
| Hypervisor | Lets you run virtual machines (Chapter 21). |
| RADIUS | Largely used by wireless to authenticate connections to the network. |
| TACACS+ | Device administration. Can control what a user may do after logging in to a device. |
| Email | Sends and receives email. |
| File | Stores a large number of files for users. |
| Database | Stores data in tables. |
| Web | Runs the web pages we browse. |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Common ports, useful when you test a service or write an ACL. DNS 53 (UDP and TCP), DHCP server 67 and client 68 (UDP), HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, TACACS+ 49 (TCP), LDAP 389, RADIUS 1812 and 1813 (UDP; older 1645 and 1646 also seen). General knowledge, not verified in this session. ADDED CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The book calls RADIUS "largely used by wireless". It is also used for wired and VPN access. In v2.0, objective 4.1 tests both TACACS+ and RADIUS for device management. UPDATED
Quick check 18.2
Q1. Which server role gives endpoints their IP address dynamically?
A. DNS
B. DHCP
C. RADIUS
D. Hypervisor
Answer: B - DHCP.
Q2. Which role controls what an administrator may do after logging in to a router?
Answer: TACACS+ - RADIUS is mostly used for network access.
Q3. What is a blade server?
Answer: A blade that plugs into a large chassis, built for redundancy and resilience - rack servers are mounted in a rack, usually 1 RU.
Book pages 498 to 507. Tracker rows: 18.3, 18.3.1, 18.3.2, 18.3.3. v1.1 objective 1.10. v2.0 objective 1.6.

The idea in plain words. Before you blame the network, check the host. You must be able to read and change the IP address, mask, default gateway and DNS server on Windows, macOS and Linux. This is useful in labs (you set the PC address to match your lab) and in real work (servers usually have static addresses, and not every subnet has DHCP). BOOK
EXAM CRITICAL
The book's Exam Essentials (p. 545): use ipconfig, ipconfig /all and ifconfig to verify IP settings on Windows, Mac and Linux. Both v1.1 (1.10) and v2.0 (1.6) test this.
18.3.1 Windows 10

GUI path (book pp. 498 to 502). Type ncpa.cpl in search or Run to open Network Connections. Right-click the adapter, choose Properties, select Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IP), then Properties. There you set the IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS servers. For IPv6, open the Version 6 properties instead. BOOK
- If you set the IP address by hand you must also set DNS by hand, because the adapter is no longer learning it from DHCP. BOOK
- Advanced lets you add more IP addresses to one adapter. It is like a secondary IP on a Cisco router interface. Useful for web servers with several sites on different IPs. BOOK
- Windows has a routing table. With more than one active adapter you can change the interface metric to prefer one. BOOK
- The DNS tab lets you add more DNS servers and append a domain suffix. With testlab.com added, typing web01 queries web01.testlab.com. BOOK

Command line (book pp. 502 to 504). ipconfig shows the IP address, mask and default gateway for each adapter. ipconfig /all adds DNS servers, MAC address and DHCP details. In PowerShell, Get-NetIPAddress shows addresses and prefix lengths (it can be filtered by interface and IPv4 only). It does not show the gateway or DNS. Use Get-DnsClientServerAddress for DNS and Get-NetRoute for routes. BOOK
Output from the book, p. 509 (shortened) BOOK
C:\> ipconfig
Ethernet adapter Local Area Connection:
Connection-specific DNS Suffix . : localdomain
Link-local IPv6 Address . . . . . : fe80::64e3:76a2:541f:ebcb%11
Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 10.1.1.1
- IPv4 Address and Subnet Mask: the host's own address. Check that it is in the same subnet as the gateway.
- Default Gateway: where the host sends traffic for other networks. It must match the router interface address. The book stresses this (p. 509).
- Link-local IPv6 Address: starts with fe80. The %11 is the interface index (zone ID). It is not part of the address.
| Task | Command (Windows) | Note |
| Show IP, mask, gateway | ipconfig | BOOK |
| Show everything incl. DNS and MAC | ipconfig /all | BOOK |
| Show the routing table | route print (or route print -4) | BOOK |
| Release and renew DHCP | ipconfig /release then ipconfig /renew | ADDED CHECK |
| Clear the DNS cache | ipconfig /flushdns | ADDED CHECK |
| Test name resolution | nslookup web01.testlab.com | ADDED CHECK |
| Show the ARP cache | arp -a | ADDED CHECK |
| Trace the path | tracert 172.16.20.254 | BOOK |
| PowerShell: addresses, DNS, routes | Get-NetIPAddress, Get-DnsClientServerAddress, Get-NetRoute | BOOK |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's route print sample has two columns swapped (p. 509). The Windows IPv4 route table columns are Network Destination, Netmask, Gateway, Interface, Metric. The Gateway column is the next-hop router and the Interface column is the host's own address. The book shows 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.1.1.10 10.1.1.1 10, which puts the PC's address in the Gateway column and the router in the Interface column. It should be 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.1.1.1 10.1.1.10 10. Status: Microsoft documentation (official, older TechNet) and several other sources agree on the column order. UPDATED
Corrected default-route line (illustrative) CHECK
C:\> route print -4
IPv4 Route Table
Network Destination Netmask Gateway Interface Metric
MEMORY TIP

Read the default route like this: destination 0.0.0.0 with mask 0.0.0.0 means "any address". The next hop is the Gateway column. The Interface column is who I am. If the Gateway column is empty or wrong, the host cannot leave its subnet.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

169.254.x.x is a clue. If ipconfig shows an address starting 169.254 the host did not get an answer from DHCP and gave itself an automatic private address (APIPA, link-local IPv4). It will only reach its own subnet. Check the VLAN, the DHCP server and any DHCP relay. ADDED CHECK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book says ipconfig is "an older command" and that PowerShell is the new way. Both work, and the exam outline names ipconfig-style checks for client OS. Learn both. The book's version of Windows (10) is out of support (see 18.1). The menus on Windows 11 differ slightly, but ncpa.cpl and the commands above still apply CHECK . UPDATED
18.3.2 macOS

GUI (book pp. 504 to 505). Open Network preferences from the Wi-Fi icon or from System Preferences. Choose the network to see the IP address. Click Advanced to see more. The TCP/IP tab sets the IP address, mask and gateway. The DNS tab adds DNS servers and works like Windows when it appends domain names. BOOK
Command line (book p. 506). ifconfig shows the IP information on a Mac and can also set an address. An address set this way will not survive a reboot. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
Menu names changed. Since macOS 13 (Ventura) the app is called System Settings, not System Preferences. The network pages moved. Status: university IT notices (secondary). UPDATED CHECK

ifconfig still works on macOS. Other handy commands: ipconfig getifaddr en0 (the IP of the Wi-Fi interface on most Macs) and networksetup -getinfo Wi-Fi (IP, mask, router). Not verified in this session. ADDED CHECK
18.3.3 Ubuntu/Red Hat

GUI (book pp. 506 to 507). Ubuntu and Red Hat family desktops (Fedora, CentOS) use the same steps. Open Settings, then Network, or click the network icon at the top right and open the connection's settings. Click the gear icon. You can change the IP address, mask, gateway and DNS servers. Press Apply. BOOK
Command line. The book says to verify with ifconfig, as on the Mac. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

ifconfig is deprecated on Linux. It belongs to the old net-tools package, which is not installed by default on Ubuntu 18.04 and later, or on newer Red Hat family systems. The current tool is ip from iproute2. On a fresh Linux VM, ifconfig may simply say "command not found". Status: several secondary sources. UPDATED CHECK
| Task | Windows | macOS | Linux (modern) |
| Show IP address | ipconfig | ifconfig | ip addr (or ip -br addr) |
| IPv6 only | ipconfig, Get-NetIPAddress | ifconfig | ip -6 addr |
| Show gateway / routes | route print | netstat -rn | ip route |
| Show DNS servers | ipconfig /all | scutil --dns | resolvectl status or /etc/resolv.conf |
| Show neighbours (ARP / NDP) | arp -a, netsh interface ipv6 show neighbor | arp -a, ndp -an | ip neigh |
| Trace the path | tracert | traceroute | traceroute (or tracepath) |
The macOS and Linux entries in this table are from general knowledge and were not verified here. ADDED CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL

Book review question 11 asks which command verifies the IP address on a Mac. The book's answer is ifconfig. Note that ipconfig is the Windows command. The question is still correct for macOS. The book's appendix has no answer printed for question 11 (it lists answers 1 to 10 only). BOOK
Quick check 18.3
Q1. A Windows PC shows IPv4 address 169.254.12.7. What happened?
Answer: It did not get an address from DHCP and used an automatic private (APIPA) address - check VLAN, DHCP server and relay.
Q2. Which route print column shows the next-hop router for the default route?
A. Network Destination
B. Netmask
C. Gateway
D. Interface
Answer: C - Gateway. The Interface column is the PC's own address.
Q3. Which Linux command replaces ifconfig for showing addresses?
Answer: ip addr - ifconfig may not even be installed.
Q4. What does the %11 after a Windows IPv6 link-local address mean?
Answer: The interface index (zone ID). It is not part of the address - you may need it when you ping a link-local address.
Book pages 507 to 522. Tracker rows: 18.4, 18.4.1, 18.4.2. v1.1 objectives 1.4 and 1.6. v2.0 objectives 1.1, 1.3, 2.4, 3.1, 3.2 and 4.6.

The idea in plain words. Troubleshooting is process of elimination. Start at the host, prove the local network works, then move outward until you find the first thing that fails. The book starts with a quick review of IP routing: if the destination is local, the host sends an ARP request; if it is remote, the host ARPs for the default gateway, sends the frame to the router, and the router looks in its routing table, picks the exit interface and builds a new frame. BOOK
Cisco's five troubleshooting steps
The book (p. 508) says the Cisco objectives give these steps when a problem is reported. BOOK
- Check the cables and interfaces for faults and verify the interface statistics.
- Make sure devices pick the correct path from source to destination. Correct the routing information if needed.
- Verify that the default gateway is correct.
- Verify that name resolution settings are correct.
- Verify that there are no access control lists (ACLs) blocking traffic.
The four host tests
| # | Test | What a pass proves | If it fails |
| 1 | ping 127.0.0.1 (loopback) | The local IP stack is working. | Problem inside the host: TCP/IP stack or OS. |
| 2 | ping the host's own IP | The IP stack is talking to the network driver (book wording). The packet does not leave the host. | NIC or driver problem, or the adapter has no address. |
| 3 | ping the default gateway | The host works on its LAN: cable, switch port, VLAN, mask and gateway address are right. | Check cable, port, VLAN, IP and mask, and the gateway address. |
| 4 | ping the remote server | The host can reach remote networks (routing works in both directions). | Use tracert to find where it stops. |
WARNING
A pass on test 2 does not prove the cable is good. The packet to your own address stays inside the host. Test 3 (the gateway) is the first test that proves the physical link. ADDED CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
The book (p. 509): it is extremely important to be able to check the default gateway on a host and confirm that it matches the router's interface address.
The book's scenario (Figure 18.16)
A manager cannot log in to Server1 from PC1. Here is the network (my table from the figure, checked with the script: all three subnets are separate and every address is in its subnet). BOOK
| Device | Interface | Address | Notes |
| PC1 | NIC | 10.1.1.10/24 | Default gateway 10.1.1.1 |
| R1 | Fa0/0 | 10.1.1.1/24 | Gateway for PC1 |
| R2 | Fa0/0 | 172.16.20.1/24 | Gateway for Server1 |
| Server1 | NIC | 172.16.20.254/24 | Default gateway 172.16.20.1 |
The walk-through, step by step. Each step narrows the problem. BOOK
| Step | What you do | Result | What it rules out |
| 1 | PC1: ipconfig, route print | IP 10.1.1.10/24, gateway 10.1.1.1. Default route present. | Wrong host IP or gateway |
| 2 | PC1: ping 127.0.0.1, then ping 10.1.1.10 | Both reply. | Local IP stack and NIC |
| 3 | PC1: ping 10.1.1.1 | Replies. | Local LAN, cabling, switch (physical and data link are fine) |
| 4 | PC1: ping 172.16.20.254 | Request timed out, 100% loss. | Local connectivity is fine; remote is not |
| 5 | PC1: tracert 172.16.20.254 | Hop 1 is 10.1.1.1, then only timeouts. | Problem is at or beyond R1 |
| 6 | R2: ping Server1 | The book says it works (its sample output contradicts itself). | Server1's LAN |
| 7 | Server1: ipconfig | 172.16.20.254/24, gateway 172.16.20.1. | Server IP and gateway |
| 8 | R2: show interface fa0/0 | 0 errors, 0 CRC, 0 collisions, full duplex, 100 Mb/s. | Interface errors on R2 Fa0/0 |
| 9 | R1: show ip route, show ip interface brief, ping R2 | Connected routes and default route via 192.168.10.254. Both interfaces up/up. Ping works. | R1 routing and link to R2 |
| 10 | R2: show ip route | S 10.1.1.0 is directly connected, FastEthernet0/0. The route to PC1's network uses the wrong exit interface. | Found the routing fault |

The routing fault. R2's static route says to reach 10.1.1.0 go out Fa0/0, which faces Server1's LAN. The path to R1 is out Fa0/1. So the echo request reaches Server1, but the reply can never get back. The book's fix: BOOK
Fix the static route (book p. 515) BOOK
R2# configure terminal
- no ip route 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 fa0/0 removes the wrong route. You must repeat it exactly as it was entered.

- ip route 10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0 192.168.10.1 adds a static route to the 10.1.1.0/24 network with R1's Fa0/1 address as the next hop. 192.168.10.1 is in R2's connected network 192.168.10.0/24, so the router can reach it.
MEMORY TIP

Always check the return path. A ping needs a route to the destination and a route back to the source. The book's fault was on the return path: PC1's request arrived, but R2 had no good route for the reply. When a ping fails, look at the routing tables on both sides. ADDED
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Exit interface vs next hop. On an Ethernet link a static route with only an exit interface makes the router ask ARP for every destination, and the neighbour must answer for it (proxy ARP). A next-hop address, or both, is the safer form. Status: general knowledge; v2.0 3.2 tests troubleshooting of static routes. ADDED CHECK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Output problem in the book (p. 511): the sample for R2#ping 172.16.20.254 shows four Windows-style "Reply" lines, then "Received = 0, Lost = 4 (100% loss)". A Cisco router prints !!!!! or ....., not Windows output, and the replies and the loss figure contradict each other. Ignore the printed result and treat the book's point as "R2 can reach Server1 locally". BOOK
Reading interface statistics
Step 1 of Cisco's method is to check interface statistics. The book (pp. 512 to 514) shows show interface fa0/0 on R2. Here are the lines that matter. BOOK
Key lines, from the book p. 512 to 513 (shortened) BOOK
R2# show interface fa0/0
FastEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
Full-duplex, 100Mb/s, 100BaseTX/FX
Input queue: 0/75/0/0 (size/max/drops/flushes); Total output drops: 0
0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles
0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
0 output errors, 0 collisions, 3 interface resets
0 babbles, 0 late collision, 0 deferred
| Counter or line | What it means | Usual causes | What to do |
| is up, line protocol is up | Layer 1 and layer 2 are working. | If down, down: cable or far end. If up, down: layer 2 problem such as encapsulation or keepalives. | Check cable and far-end port. |
| Speed and duplex | What the two ends negotiated or were set to. | Mismatch, or autonegotiation failure. | See the duplex rule below. |
| Input queue drops, ignored, throttles | More traffic arrives than the router can process. BOOK | Overload, CPU, traffic bursts. | Find when it rises; check CPU. |
| Output queue drops | Packets dropped because of interface congestion. VoIP suffers. BOOK | Congestion. | If constant, consider QoS. |
| Input errors | Total of bad received frames, such as CRC. BOOK | Cabling, hardware, duplex mismatch. | Check cable, then duplex. |
| CRC | Frame arrived with a bad checksum. | Bad cable, noise, or the full-duplex side of a duplex mismatch. | Replace cable; check duplex. |
| Runts, giants | Frames that are too small or too big. | Collisions or duplex mismatch (runts). MTU or tagging mismatch (giants). ADDED CHECK | Check duplex and MTU. |

| Output errors, collisions, late collision | Frames that failed to send. Late collisions are collisions after the first 64 bytes. | Duplex mismatch (seen on the half-duplex side); cable too long. | Fix duplex. |
| Interface resets, lost carrier | The link dropped and came back. ADDED | Loose cable, bad port, flapping link. | Check physical layer. |

Speed and duplex. The book says the most common cause of interface errors is a mismatched duplex mode between two ends. Mismatched speed means the link will not come up. Mismatched duplex means the link comes up but with a "legion of errors", slow performance, intermittent connectivity or even no communication. A telling sign is that the late collision counter increments. BOOK
Set speed and duplex by hand if autonegotiation fails (book p. 513) BOOK
Switch(config)# interface gi0/1
Switch(config-if)# speed 1000
Switch(config-if)# duplex full
- interface gi0/1 selects the port.
- speed 1000 forces 1000 Mbps. The options are 10, 100, 1000 and auto.

| Function | Message | Sent to | What it does |
| Router solicitation (RS) | ICMPv6 type 133 CHECK | FF02::2 (all routers) | A host asks routers to announce themselves. |
| Router advertisement (RA) | type 134 CHECK | FF02::1 (all nodes) or unicast to the asking host | A router gives the prefix and default gateway. |
| Neighbour solicitation (NS) | type 135 CHECK | Solicited-node multicast of the target | "I need your MAC address." Also used for DAD. |
| Neighbour advertisement (NA) | type 136 CHECK | The asker (unicast) or all nodes | "Here is my MAC address." |
| Redirect | type 137 CHECK | The host | A router points the host to a better first hop. |
| Duplicate address detection (DAD) | NS for the host's own new address | Solicited-node multicast | Checks nobody else already uses the address. ADDED CHECK |
Remember: RS and RA are about routers; NS and NA are about hosts. A neighbour is a device on the same data link or VLAN. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

One sentence is wrong. The book says hosts send an RS asking routers to respond, "which they do using the multicast address FF02::2" (p. 524). The RS is sent to FF02::2. Routers answer with an RA sent to FF02::1 or unicast to the host, as the book's next sentence says. UPDATED
Solicited-node multicast address

The address is FF02::1:FF followed by the last 24 bits of the unicast address (the book writes it as FF02:0:0:0:0:1:FF/104). BOOK Every host joins the group for each of its addresses. Example (script-checked): fe80::64e3:76a2:541f:ebcb ends in 1f:ebcb, so its solicited-node address is ff02::1:ff1f:ebcb, and the multicast MAC is 33-33-ff-1f-eb-cb. That is exactly what appears in the book's netsh table. ADDED
The book also says IGMP's job (a host telling its router it joins a multicast group) is replaced by multicast listener discovery (MLD), which is part of ICMPv6. BOOK
The neighbor cache and its states
Output from the book, p. 528 BOOK
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
IPv6 Address Age Link-layer Addr State Interface
| State | Book's meaning | Clearer version (Cisco IOS text) |
| INCMP (incomplete) | Address resolution is being done. An NS was sent but no reply yet. | Same. |
| REACH (reachable) | Positive confirmation received. The path works. REACH is good. | Confirmation received within the last reachable time. |
| STALE | No communication within the reachable time. Goes back to REACH on the next communication. | Reachability unknown. No action is taken until a packet is sent to the neighbour. |

| DELAY | After STALE, no confirmation within DELAY_FIRST_PROBE_TIME. UPDATED | A packet was sent to a STALE neighbour. Wait about 5 seconds for upper-layer confirmation. If none, send an NS and go to PROBE. |
| PROBE | The interface resends an NS and waits for confirmation. | Same: NS sent repeatedly until confirmation. |
Status: the Cisco IOS neighbour state text was found quoted in a Cisco Community post; the 5-second default comes from secondary sources. CHECK
EXAM CRITICAL
Book review questions 1, 5 and 6 test this: REACH = path confirmed working; STALE = not communicated within the reachable time; show ipv6 neighbors is the IPv6 ARP cache.
Quick check 18.5.1
Q1. Which multicast address does a host send a router solicitation to?
Answer: B - FF02::2 (all routers). Routers answer with an RA.
Q2. What is the solicited-node multicast address of a host whose address ends in ...:3ab7, with last 24 bits 11:3ab7?
Answer: FF02::1:FF11:3AB7 - FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits.
Q3. An IPv6 neighbour entry is STALE. A packet is now sent to that neighbour. What state comes next?
Answer: DELAY, then PROBE if no confirmation arrives - if the neighbour confirms, it returns to REACH.

Book pages 531 to 544. Tracker rows: 18.6, 18.6.1, 18.6.2. v1.1 objectives 2.1, 2.2.a, 2.2.b, 2.2.c. v2.0 objectives 2.1.b, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4. This section builds on Chapter 8 (VLANs and trunks). If any command here is new, read Chapter 8 first.

The idea in plain words. VLANs break up broadcast domains. A port joins a VLAN with switchport access vlan. If two hosts in the same VLAN sit on different switches, the link between the switches must be a trunk (or an access port in that same VLAN). There are two kinds of fault: a VLAN fault (the port, or the VLAN itself, is wrong on one switch) and a trunk fault (the link between switches is wrong). The book uses Figure 18.22: PC1 on S1 Gi0/1 and PC2 on S1 Gi0/2, and PC3 on S2 Gi0/3, all in VLAN 10 (192.168.10.1, .2, .3). S1 and S2 are joined by Gi0/13 and Gi0/14. BOOK
| Host | Switch and port | VLAN | Address |
| Inter-switch links | S1 Gi0/13 and Gi0/14 to S2 Gi0/13 and Gi0/14 | trunk wanted | n/a |
18.6.1 VLAN Troubleshooting
Book pp. 532 to 537. Tracker row: 18.6.1.
Check VLANs when you lose connectivity between hosts, and when you add a new host to a VLAN and it does not work. The book's three steps: BOOK
- Verify the VLAN database on all your switches (show vlan).
- Verify the CAM table (the MAC address table): show mac address-table.
- Verify the port VLAN assignments: show interfaces <int> switchport and switchport access vlan <id>.
The scenario
A manager says they cannot reach the new sales team member. Sales is VLAN 10. BOOK
| Step | Switch and command | What the book found | Meaning |
| 1 | S1: show vlan | VLAN 10 Sales exists. Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 are in it. | S1 is fine so far. |
| 2 | S1: show mac address-table | Two dynamic MACs in VLAN 10, learned on Gi0/1 and Gi0/2. | PC1 and PC2 are connected and seen. S1 looks good. |
| 3 | S2: show interfaces gi0/3 switchport | Access Mode VLAN: 10 (Inactive) | The port is set to VLAN 10 but the VLAN is inactive. |
| 4 | S2: show mac address-table | No dynamic MAC on Gi0/3. | The switch cannot learn PC3 on an inactive VLAN. |
| 5 | S2: show vlan brief | VLAN 10 is not in the database. | Found the fault. |
S2 port Gi0/3 (book p. 534, shortened) BOOK
S2# show interfaces gi0/3 switchport
Name: Gi0/3
Switchport: Enabled
Administrative Mode: dynamic desirable
Operational Mode: static access
Negotiation of Trunking: On
Access Mode VLAN: 10 (Inactive)
Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 1 (default)
- Administrative Mode dynamic desirable is what is configured: the port would like to trunk if it meets a switch. The book points out that we are using it as an access port.
- Operational Mode static access is what the port is really doing.
- Access Mode VLAN: 10 (Inactive) is the clue. A port in a VLAN that does not exist on this switch is inactive. No traffic flows.
The fix and the proof (book p. 535) BOOK
S2# configure terminal
S2(config)# vlan 10
S2(config-vlan)# name Sales
S2# show mac address-table
10 001a.6c46.9b09 DYNAMIC Gi0/3
- vlan 10 and name Sales create the missing VLAN in S2's database. The port becomes active.

- The MAC address of PC3 now shows up in VLAN 10 on Gi0/3. That is the proof. If the port had been in the wrong VLAN instead, you would fix it with interface gi0/3, then switchport access vlan 10. BOOK

After the fix, PC1 can ping PC2 (same switch) but cannot ping PC3 (other switch). So the VLAN database and port assignments are now right. The next suspect is the link between the switches: a trunk problem. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The first MAC in show mac address-table is not the switch's base MAC. The book says (p. 534) that the first address listed (0100.0ccc.cccc STATIC CPU) "is the base MAC address of the switch and is used by STP in the bridge ID". It is not. 0100.0ccc.cccc is a Cisco multicast address used by CDP, VTP, DTP, PAgP and UDLD. Frames sent to it go to the CPU. A different address in the table (0100.0ccc.cccd) is for Cisco's shared spanning tree. Status: a Cisco document on reserved addresses lists CDP at 01-00-0c-cc-cc-cc (official); Cisco Community confirms the rest. UPDATED
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Typos in the book's VLAN scenario. The text refers to "Figure 18.5" (it means Figure 18.22) and to "Gi/013" (Gi0/13). The command S1#sh interfaces gi0/1 trunk is typed for port Gi0/1, but the discussion is about Gi0/13. The book also says to correct VLAN membership with the "switch access vlan" command; the real command is switchport access vlan. BOOK
| Command | Use it to see |
| show vlan or show vlan brief | Which VLANs exist and which access ports are in each. Trunk ports are not listed. |
| show vlan id 10 | Just one VLAN. ADDED CHECK |
| show mac address-table | Which MAC address was learned on which port and VLAN. |
| show mac address-table vlan 10 | Only the MACs of one VLAN. ADDED CHECK |
| show interfaces gi0/3 switchport | Administrative and operational mode, access VLAN (and whether it is Inactive), voice VLAN, native VLAN. |
| show interfaces status | Port state, VLAN, duplex and speed in one table. ADDED CHECK |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Other causes of "host in the VLAN cannot talk". The port is shut down or error-disabled; the VLAN exists but is suspended or shut down (state suspend or shutdown under the VLAN); the host has the wrong IP or mask for the VLAN's subnet; the port is a trunk, not access; the voice VLAN is missing for a phone. Status: general knowledge. ADDED CHECK
Quick check 18.6.1
Q1. A port shows Access Mode VLAN: 20 (Inactive). What do you check first?
Answer: Whether VLAN 20 exists on this switch (show vlan brief). Create it if it is missing - an inactive VLAN means the database lacks it.
Q2. Why does a host not appear in the MAC address table?
Answer: Its port is down, in an inactive VLAN, or the host is silent. Check port state and VLAN - the switch learns MACs from received frames.
Q3. Which command shows the access VLAN, native VLAN and operational mode of one port?
Answer: show interfaces <int> switchport - show vlan does not show trunk ports.
18.6.2 Trunk Troubleshooting
Book pp. 537 to 544. Tracker row: 18.6.2.

Troubleshoot trunks when hosts in the same VLAN on different switches cannot talk. The book says Cisco calls this "VLAN leaking". I could not confirm that term in a Cisco source. BOOK CHECK The book's steps and commands: BOOK
- Verify that the interface configuration is set to the correct trunk parameters.
- Verify that the ports are configured correctly.
- Verify the native VLAN on each switch.

Commands: show interfaces trunk, show vlan, show interfaces <int> trunk, show interfaces <int> switchport, show dtp interface <int>, switchport mode, switchport mode dynamic, switchport trunk native vlan <id>. BOOK
Finding the fault: the ports are access ports
| Step | Switch and command | What the book found | Meaning |
| 1 | S2: show interfaces trunk | No output at all. | No trunks on S2. |

| 2 | S1 and S2: show vlan brief | Gi0/13 and Gi0/14 are listed under VLAN 1. | A port in the show vlan list is an access port, so the inter-switch links are access ports in VLAN 1 and pass VLAN 1 only. |
| 3 | S1: show interfaces gi0/13 switchport | Admin mode dynamic auto, operational mode static access. | The port is not trunking. |
| 4 | S1: show interfaces gi0/1 trunk | Mode auto, status not-trunking, native VLAN 1. | Confirmed. (The book typed Gi0/1 here; Gi0/13 is meant.) |
| 5 | S1 and S2: show dtp interface gi0/13 | S1 and S2: ACCESS/AUTO/ACCESS, DTP hello timers running. | Both ends are auto and waiting. |

The book's explanation: "it's not that they're running in access mode; it's because two ports in dynamic auto will not form a trunk!" This is a really common problem because most Cisco switches ship in dynamic auto. BOOK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

The book is consistent here and contradicts its Chapter 8. In this section (p. 541) and in the review answer to question 10 ("Most Cisco switches ship with a default port mode of auto"), the book says the default is dynamic auto. In Chapter 8 it said dynamic desirable is the default on all new switches. The Chapter 18 statement is the correct one. See the Chapter 8 manual. BOOK UPDATED
DTP status (book p. 540) BOOK
S1# show dtp interface gi0/13
DTP information for GigabitEthernet0/13:
TOS/TAS/TNS: ACCESS/AUTO/ACCESS
TOT/TAT/TNT: NATIVE/NEGOTIATE/NATIVE
Neighbor address 1: 00211C910D8D
Neighbor address 2: 000000000000
Hello timer expiration (sec/state): 12/RUNNING
Access timer expiration (sec/state): never/STOPPED

- The first line (TOS/TAS/TNS) is read as trunk operating status, administrative status and negotiation status. Here ACCESS/AUTO/ACCESS means the port is operating as access, configured as auto. The second line (TOT/TAT/TNT) is the same for the trunk type (encapsulation). I am reading these abbreviations from memory; the book does not explain them. ADDED CHECK
- Neighbor address 1 is the MAC address of the neighbour's DTP speaker. A neighbour that is not sending DTP shows all zeros (see S2's output in the book, p. 541).
MEMORY TIP
Use show dtp interface <int> to see what DTP thinks. It is the answer to book review question 3. The wrong answers all invent a command.
The five DTP modes (book p. 540)
| Mode | Book's description |
| Access | Trunking is not allowed on the port. |
| Auto (dynamic auto) | Will trunk only if the remote port is on (trunk) or desirable. Creates the trunk when the neighbour asks. |
| Desirable (dynamic desirable) | Will trunk with all modes except access. Sends DTP to say it is trying to become a trunk. |
| Nonegotiate | No DTP frames are generated. Only use when the neighbour is manually set to trunk or access. |
| Trunk (on) | Trunks with all modes except access. Always trunking, regardless of the neighbour. |

Use the negotiation table in the Chapter 8 manual (8.4.2) for the full matrix. The book says Cisco recommends not using DTP and configuring ports manually, and the author agrees. BOOK The book's switchport mode ? list also shows dot1q-tunnel (802.1Q tunnelling) and private-vlan, which are beyond the CCNA. BOOK
The fix: make one end desirable
Book pp. 541 to 542 (shortened) BOOK
S2(config)# interface gi0/13
S2(config-if)# switchport mode dynamic desirable
S2(config-if)# do show interfaces trunk
Port Mode Encapsulation Status Native vlan
Gi0/13 desirable n-isl trunking 1
S2(config-if)# interface gi0/14
S2(config-if)# switchport mode dynamic desirable
- switchport mode dynamic desirable makes S2 ask for a trunk. S1 is auto, so it accepts. You only need to fix one side because auto trunks with desirable or on. BOOK
- The log lines show the line protocol going down and up as the link changes to a trunk. This is normal.
- Encapsulation n-isl means the two switches negotiated ISL. The book dislikes this because ISL cannot send untagged frames, so it has no native VLAN.
MEMORY TIP
Better fix: set both ends to switchport mode trunk with switchport nonegotiate, and set the encapsulation to 802.1Q where the switch offers a choice. Then nothing depends on DTP. ADDED
Changing the native VLAN, and the mismatch
The book then changes the native VLAN on S1 to 392. On an ISL trunk the command is refused: Port is not 802.1Q trunk, no action. So the author changes the encapsulation on S1 to 802.1Q. BOOK
Book pp. 542 to 543 (shortened) BOOK
S1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 392
Port is not 802.1Q trunk, no action
S1(config-if)# interface range gi0/13 - 14
S1(config-if-range)# switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on
GigabitEthernet0/13 (392), with S2 GigabitEthernet0/13 (1).
- switchport trunk native vlan 392 sets the untagged VLAN. It was refused because ISL has no native VLAN.
- switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q forces 802.1Q. DTP then moves the neighbour to 802.1Q too (n-802.1q on S2). This command exists only on switches that support both methods.
- %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH appears because S1 now uses VLAN 392 while S2 still uses VLAN 1.
Spot the mismatch (book p. 543, shortened) BOOK
S1# show interfaces trunk
Port Mode Encapsulation Status Native vlan
Gi0/13 auto 802.1q trunking 392
Gi0/14 auto 802.1q trunking 1
S2# show interfaces trunk
Gi0/13 desirable n-802.1q trunking 1
Gi0/14 desirable n-802.1q trunking 1

Compare the Native vlan column on both switches: Gi0/13 is 392 on S1 and 1 on S2. That is the mismatch. The show interfaces gi0/13 switchport output also shows it: S1 shows Trunking Native Mode VLAN: 392 (Inactive), S2 shows 1 (default). BOOK
Make both ends match (book p. 544) BOOK
S2(config)# interface gi0/13
S2(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 392
S2# show interfaces trunk
Gi0/13 desirable n-802.1q trunking 392
- After the encapsulation change, PC1 can ping PC3 (!!!!!). The tagged VLAN 10 traffic crosses the trunk. BOOK

- The book says you can have different native VLANs on different links and each link still works, but it is best to have them the same for management. The rule that matters is that both ends of each link match. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book again says a native VLAN mismatch is mostly harmless (p. 544). It says the mismatch "only means you can't send untagged frames down the link", essentially management frames like CDP, and "it's not the end of the world". In Chapter 8 the same claim was found to be wrong: under PVST+ a mismatch can put the port into a PVID-inconsistent state that blocks traffic in the affected VLANs, and untagged frames can leak into a different VLAN at the other end. The book's own ping working is not proof the mismatch is harmless; it only shows VLAN 10 was not blocked on that link in that test. Fix both ends. Status: Cisco document on PVID inconsistency (official). UPDATED CHECK
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

392 (Inactive). The book does not explain this. The native VLAN 392 was never created on S1, so S1 reports the native VLAN as inactive. Create the native VLAN on both switches, or use one that already exists. I did not test what an inactive native VLAN does on real equipment. ADDED CHECK
| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| show interfaces trunk shows nothing | Ports are access ports | Configure a trunk: switchport mode trunk (both ends). |
| not-trunking, admin mode auto both ends | auto + auto | Make one end desirable, or better both ends trunk. |
| Port is not 802.1Q trunk when setting native VLAN | Link negotiated ISL | Set switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q. |
| %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH | Different native VLAN at each end | Make both ends the same. |
| Trunk up, one VLAN does not cross | VLAN missing, not allowed, or not forwarding | show interfaces trunk: check the allowed and active lists. |
Quick check 18.6.2
Q1. Which command shows the DTP status of an interface?
A. show dtp status
B. show dtp interface <int>
C. show interface <int> dtp
D. show dtp status interface <int>
Answer: B - show dtp interface <int>.
Q2. Which two commands help you spot a native VLAN mismatch?
Answer: show interfaces trunk and show interfaces <int> switchport - compare the native VLAN on both switches.
Q3. Which port mode generates no DTP frames?
A. Auto
B. Desirable
C. Nonegotiate
D. Trunk (without nonegotiate)
Answer: C - Nonegotiate. It is allowed only when the port is manually set to trunk or access.
Q4. Two new switches are cabled together and both ports are at the default. They did not trunk. Why?
Answer: Both ports are dynamic auto; neither end asks for a trunk - set one end to desirable or trunk.

content.text: This is the whole chapter in one table. Work from the top: the earlier a row, the closer to the host. None of this was tested on hardware. Treat "First check" as a starting point. CHECK
| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |
| PC has an address starting 169.254 | DHCP did not answer | ipconfig /all; VLAN of the port; DHCP server; relay |
| ping 127.0.0.1 fails | Broken local IP stack | Fix the OS TCP/IP stack or NIC driver |
| Own IP replies, gateway does not | Cable, port, VLAN, wrong mask or gateway address | show interfaces status, show vlan brief; compare host and gateway subnets |
| Gateway replies, remote does not | Routing fault (often the return path), or an ACL | tracert; show ip route on the gateway and on the far router; extended ping with a source |
| Remote ping works, TCP application fails | ACL or firewall blocks the port, or service is down | show access-lists; show ip interface <int> (which ACL, which direction); test the port |
| Works by IP, not by name | DNS or host table | nslookup; DNS server on the host; ip host on routers |
| tracert stops at the first hop | The gateway has no route onward | show ip route on the gateway |
| Slow, intermittent, CRC and late collisions | Duplex mismatch (or bad cable) | show interfaces: duplex on both ends; clear counters and watch |
| Link will not come up between two ends | Speed mismatch or bad cable | show interfaces; speed on both ends |
| IPv6: host has no default gateway | No RA: ipv6 unicast-routing missing, or RAs blocked | show ipv6 interface <int>; ipconfig on the host |
| IPv6: ping to link-local fails on Windows | Zone ID missing | Add %<index> to the address |
| IPv6 static route rejected | Link-local next hop without exit interface | Use the fully specified form |
| IPv6 ping one way only | Missing or wrong route on the return path | show ipv6 route on both routers; check next-hop addresses against show ipv6 interface brief |
| Port shows Access Mode VLAN: N (Inactive) | VLAN does not exist on this switch | show vlan brief; create the VLAN |
| Same-VLAN hosts on two switches cannot talk | Trunk missing, VLAN not allowed or missing on one switch | show interfaces trunk; show vlan brief on both |
| No trunk, both ends dynamic auto | auto + auto | show dtp interface <int>; set one end desirable or both ends trunk |
| %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH | Native VLANs differ | Compare the Native vlan column in show interfaces trunk on both switches; fix both |
| Port is not 802.1Q trunk, no action | Trunk negotiated ISL | switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q |
| Topic | Remember |

| Client OS commands | Windows ipconfig, ipconfig /all, route print, tracert, Get-NetIPAddress. macOS ifconfig. Linux ip addr (ifconfig is old). In route print: Gateway = next hop, Interface = my address. |
| Four host tests | 127.0.0.1, own IP, default gateway, remote host. Gateway test is the first to prove the physical LAN. |
| Cisco five steps | Cables and interface stats; correct path (routing); default gateway; name resolution; ACLs. |

| Interface counters | Late collisions: half-duplex side of a mismatch. CRC and runts on a full-duplex port: duplex mismatch or bad cable. Output queue drops: congestion. Both ends auto or both fixed. |
| Return path | A ping needs a route there and back. Extended ping with source tests the return path. |
| Static routes | Prefer a next hop. An exit interface on Ethernet relies on ARP for every destination. IPv6 link-local next hop needs the exit interface. |

| ACLs | Top-down, first match, implicit deny. Extended: closest to the source. show access-lists, show ip interface. Edit with sequence numbers (named and numbered). ACLs do not filter traffic the router creates. |
| Name resolution | Works by IP but not by name: DNS or host table. nslookup, ip host. |
| SPAN | Copies source port traffic to a destination port. Destination carries only copied traffic by default. Low exam priority. |

| IPv6 troubleshooting | Same five steps. Each interface has link-local and global addresses. Host gateway = router link-local from an RA. Router needs ipv6 unicast-routing. show ipv6 neighbors, show ipv6 route, show ipv6 interface brief. |
| ICMPv6 and NDP | NS/NA replace ARP. RS to FF02::2, RA to FF02::1. Solicited-node = FF02::1:FF + last 24 bits. Next Header 58. States: INCMP, REACH, STALE, DELAY, PROBE. |
| EUI-64 | Insert FF:FE in the middle of the MAC; flip the 7th bit of the first byte. |
| VLAN troubleshooting | show vlan brief (access ports only), show mac address-table, show interfaces <int> switchport. Inactive VLAN = missing from the database. |

| Trunk troubleshooting | show interfaces trunk (empty = no trunks), show dtp interface. auto + auto = no trunk. ISL negotiated = no native VLAN. Native VLAN mismatch: compare both ends; can block VLANs, not only CDP. |
| Book wording to avoid | SVI is not fa0/0; switchport trunk native vlan (not switchport native vlan); show ip route (not show route). |

content.text: VERIFY

Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware, in Packet Tracer, or on Windows, macOS or Linux clients. All outputs not copied from the book are expectations. Record what you actually see in the labs and update the tracker.

Use Cisco Packet Tracer (or another lab tool). Packet Tracer can behave differently from real equipment, and I could not run it here. Every output below is what you should expect, not something I saw. CHECK After each lab, write down what you actually saw in the tracker table at the end. That record is the evidence for changing a status. Labs 1, 2 and 4 are "find the fault" labs: build the working network first, save a copy, then break it (or ask someone to) and troubleshoot with the method.

Goal: practise the host tests, tracert, routing and ACL checks. Topology: the book's Figure 18.16: PC1 and switch S1 on R1 Gi0/0; R1 Gi0/1 to R2 Gi0/1; R2 Gi0/0 to switch S2 and Server1 (turn on the HTTP service on Server1). Use 1941 routers (Gi0/0, Gi0/1) and 2960 switches. All subnets were checked by script: no overlaps.
| Device | Interface | Address | Gateway |
Step A: build the working network
Lab 1 working configuration CHECK
R1(config)# interface gi0/0
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.1.1.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gi0/1
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# exit
R2(config)# interface gi0/1
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# interface gi0/0
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
R2(config-if)# exit
- Each ip address and no shutdown brings up an interface in its subnet.
- R1's default route sends everything unknown to R2. R2's static route sends traffic for PC1's network to R1 (next hop 192.168.10.1).
Check it works: PC1 pings 172.16.20.254 and opens http://172.16.20.254 in the browser. Save the file.
Step B: plant fault 1 (the book's routing fault)
Fault 1: wrong exit interface CHECK
Now troubleshoot from PC1 without looking at the commands above. Do the four host tests, tracert, then show ip route on R1 and R2. Fix it with a next-hop route.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. PC1 pings 127.0.0.1, its own IP and the gateway 10.1.1.1, but the ping to 172.16.20.254 times out. tracert shows the first hop 10.1.1.1 and then timeouts. On R2, show ip route shows S 10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0, which is the wrong interface. Why it fails: the request reaches Server1, but R2 sends the reply out Gi0/0 instead of toward R1. After the fix the ping works. Try ping 10.1.1.10 source 172.16.20.1 from R2 before and after the fix to test the return path. Packet Tracer may print routes or traceroute lines differently. CHECK
Step C: plant fault 2 (an ACL that passes ICMP only)
Fault 2 CHECK
R2(config)# access-list 110 permit icmp any any
R2(config)# interface gi0/0
R2(config-if)# ip access-group 110 out
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. Ping to Server1 works but the web browser fails. show access-lists on R2 shows 10 permit icmp any any with a rising match count. show ip interface gi0/0 shows Outgoing access list is 110. Fix: interface gi0/0, no ip access-group 110 out, then no access-list 110. Packet Tracer may show the ACL line differently. CHECK
Step D: plant fault 3 (wrong gateway on the server)
Set Server1's default gateway to 172.16.2.1. Find it with ipconfig and with the subnet check: 172.16.2.1 is not in 172.16.20.0/24 (calculated). This is the book's review question 8. Fix and re-test.
Record in the tracker: for each fault, which test or command first pointed to it, and the fix.

labs.title: A named extended ACL, with a planted bug

content.text: Goal: write, test and edit an extended ACL. Topology: the working Lab 1 network (remove any fault ACLs first).
- On R1 create the ACL with the wrong source on purpose (below) and apply it inbound on Gi0/0.
- From PC1 open http://172.16.20.254. It should still work. Check show access-lists.
- Fix line 10 with its sequence number. Test again from PC1.
- Check the hit counters and show ip interface gi0/0.
- Edit a numbered ACL: create ip access-list extended 120, add one line, then insert a line with sequence number 5.
Lab 2 ACL and its fix CHECK
R1(config)# ip access-list extended Block_Web
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny tcp host 10.1.1.1 host 172.16.20.254 eq 80
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip any any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface gi0/0
R1(config-if)# ip access-group Block_Web in
R1(config)# ip access-list extended Block_Web
R1(config-ext-nacl)# no 10
R1(config-ext-nacl)# 10 deny tcp host 10.1.1.10 host 172.16.20.254 eq 80
- deny tcp host 10.1.1.1 ... eq 80 has the wrong source (R1's own address). The traffic comes from 10.1.1.10, so nothing matches.
- permit ip any any stops the implicit deny from dropping everything else.
- no 10 removes only line 10. 10 deny ... inserts the corrected line at the same position.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. With the bug, the browser still works and line 10 shows no matches. After the fix, the browser from PC1 fails while ping still works. The hit counter on line 10 rises with each browser attempt and line 20 counts the ICMP and other traffic. show ip interface gi0/0 shows Inbound access list is Block_Web. Packet Tracer ACL display and sequence-number editing may differ from real IOS. CHECK

Think about it. A web request started on R1 itself (for example telnet 172.16.20.254 80 typed on R1) is not filtered by an inbound ACL on Gi0/0. Try it and compare with the book's test on p. 521. Record what you see. CHECK

Goal: repeat the book's IPv6 scenario with your own addressing, and practise the link-local next-hop rule. Topology: PC1, R1, R2, Server1 as in Lab 1 (switches optional). All /64s were checked by script: no overlaps. CHECK
| Device | Interface | Address | Notes |
| R1 | Gi0/0 | 2001:DB8:ACAD:3::1/64 | PC1's LAN. Link-local FE80::1 |
| R1 | Gi0/1 | 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::1/64 | Link to R2. Link-local FE80::1 |
| R2 | Gi0/1 | 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::2/64 | Link to R1. Link-local FE80::2 |
| R2 | Gi0/0 | 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1/64 | Server1's LAN. Link-local FE80::2 |
| PC1 | NIC | SLAAC (automatic) | Gets prefix and gateway from the RA |
| Server1 | NIC | 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::10/64 | Gateway FE80::2 (or 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::1) |
- Configure the routers (below). Set PC1 to automatic IPv6 and Server1 as in the table.
- On PC1 run ipconfig. Note the address and the default gateway. Is the gateway the link-local address?
- From PC1 ping the gateway, then ping R1 Gi0/1, then ping Server1. It should fail at the last step. Find out why with show ipv6 route on both routers.
- Add the routes. First use the global next hop, test, then replace it with the link-local form (and try it without the interface to see the error).
- Run show ipv6 neighbors on R1 after the ping. Note the state of each entry.
- Turn off ipv6 unicast-routing on R1 and renew PC1's IPv6 settings. What happens to the gateway?
Lab 3 configuration CHECK
R1(config)# ipv6 unicast-routing
R1(config)# interface gi0/0
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:3::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address FE80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
R1(config-if)# interface gi0/1
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::1/64
R1(config-if)# ipv6 address FE80::1 link-local
R1(config-if)# no shutdown
(repeat on R2 with ::2 / FE80::2 on Gi0/1 and ::1 / FE80::2 on Gi0/0)
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::2
R2(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:3::/64 2001:DB8:ACAD:2::1
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:DB8:ACAD:1::/64 gi0/1 FE80::2
- ipv6 unicast-routing turns routing and router advertisements on. Without it PC1 gets no gateway.
- ipv6 address ... link-local sets an easy-to-read link-local address, FE80::1. It only has to be unique on the link.
- ipv6 route <prefix>/64 <global next hop> needs no interface. The link-local form gi0/1 FE80::2 does.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. PC1 gets a global address in 2001:db8:acad:3::/64 and a default gateway of FE80::1. Before the routes, the ping to R1 works and the ping to Server1 fails. After the routes both work. show ipv6 neighbors shows REACH (and possibly STALE or DELAY after a pause). Typing the link-local route without gi0/1 is rejected with a message asking for the interface. With ipv6 unicast-routing off on R1, PC1 should lose its gateway after the next RA lifetime or renew. Packet Tracer may not match real IOS on all of these. CHECK

labs.title: VLAN and trunk faults between two switches

content.text: Goal: find the three faults of 18.6. Topology: S1 and S2 (2960) joined by Gi0/1 on both. PC1 (192.168.10.11) and PC2 (192.168.10.12) on S1 Fa0/1 and Fa0/2. PC3 (192.168.10.13) on S2 Fa0/1. All /24, VLAN 10 Sales. Do Chapter 8 Lab 2 first if the commands are new.
Lab 4 build, then fault 1 (delete the VLAN on S2) CHECK
S1(config)# vlan 10
S1(config-vlan)# name Sales
S1(config-vlan)# interface range fa0/1 - 2
S1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
S2(config)# vlan 10
S2(config-vlan)# name Sales
S2(config-vlan)# interface fa0/1
S2(config-if)# switchport mode access
S2(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
S2(config-if)# exit
S2(config)# no vlan 10
- Fault 1: no vlan 10 on S2. On S2 run show interfaces fa0/1 switchport and show vlan brief. Fix with vlan 10. Check show mac address-table.

- Fault 2: leave both Gi0/1 ports at the default (dynamic auto). Ping PC1 to PC3. Run show interfaces trunk and show dtp interface gi0/1 on both. Fix: set S2 Gi0/1 to switchport mode dynamic desirable. Check show interfaces trunk again.
- Fault 3: create VLAN 99 on both switches. On S1 Gi0/1 enter switchport trunk native vlan 99. Read the log message. Compare show interfaces trunk on both switches. Fix S2 to match.
- Finally replace DTP with a static design: switchport mode trunk and switchport nonegotiate on both ends, native VLAN 99 on both.
MEMORY TIP

Expected results. Fault 1: the port shows Access Mode VLAN: 10 (Inactive), VLAN 10 is missing from show vlan brief, PC3 is missing from the MAC table. After the fix PC3 appears in VLAN 10. Fault 2: show interfaces trunk is empty, show dtp interface shows an access/auto state on both ends; after the fix a trunk with n-802.1q appears and PC1 reaches PC3. Fault 3: a %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH message names both ports and VLANs; the Native vlan columns differ. Packet Tracer 2960 behaviour with DTP, CDP and native VLAN logs may differ from real switches. CHECK

labs.title: Lab 5 (paper): read the counters, calculate EUI-64

content.text: Part A: interface counters. Say what each case suggests and what you would do. Answers are below.
| Case | Output | Your diagnosis |
| A | Half-duplex, 100Mb/s, 0 CRC, 412 late collision, 640 collisions |  |
| B | Full-duplex, 100Mb/s, 5,120 CRC, 3,300 runts, 0 collisions |  |
| C | Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, 0 errors, input queue drops 1,200, output queue drops 0 |  |

Answers: A: this is the half-duplex side of a duplex mismatch (late collisions), so check the neighbour: it is probably hard-set to full. Set both ends to auto, or both to the same fixed value. B: the full-duplex side of a duplex mismatch (CRC and runts, no collisions), or a bad cable; check the neighbour's duplex first, then replace the cable. C: the device receives more traffic than it can process; find when the counter rises and check CPU. The counters are made-up examples for practice. CHECK

Part B: EUI-64 and solicited-node. An interface has MAC 00-1B-44-11-3A-B7 and prefix 2001:db8:acad:10::/64. Work out: the global address, the link-local address, the solicited-node multicast address, and the multicast MAC address. Then check yourself.

Answer (calculated by script): global 2001:db8:acad:10:21b:44ff:fe11:3ab7; link-local fe80::21b:44ff:fe11:3ab7; solicited-node ff02::1:ff11:3ab7; multicast MAC 33-33-ff-11-3a-b7. Method: insert FF:FE in the middle of the MAC, flip the 7th bit of the first byte (00 becomes 02).

Part C (optional): SPAN. If your Packet Tracer switch supports it, configure monitor session 1 source interface fa0/1 and monitor session 1 destination interface fa0/3, then verify with show monitor session 1. Some versions do not support SPAN. Record whether yours did. CHECK

quizzes.title: Troubleshooting IP, IPv6, and VLANs — review questions

questions.source: Q1. Why is an access point also called an endpoint?
questions.q: Why is an access point also called an endpoint?
questions.why: It connects to the network (usually by wire) like any other device, even though it provides wireless access to others - vendors count it as an endpoint.

questions.source: Q2. Why do office PCs often plug into the IP phone instead of the wall?
questions.q: Why do office PCs often plug into the IP phone instead of the wall?
questions.why: To save cabling and switch ports. The phone has a built-in switch - this is why the switch port carries a data VLAN and a voice VLAN.

questions.source: Q3. Which endpoint types use wireless only, according to the book?
questions.q: Which endpoint types use wireless only, according to the book?
questions.why: Mobile phones and tablets - desktops and laptops can use either.

questions.source: Q1. Which server role gives endpoints their IP address dynamically?
questions.q: Which server role gives endpoints their IP address dynamically?
questions.why: DHCP.

questions.source: Q2. Which role controls what an administrator may do after logging in to a router?
questions.q: Which role controls what an administrator may do after logging in to a router?
questions.why: TACACS+ - RADIUS is mostly used for network access.

questions.source: Q3. What is a blade server?
questions.q: What is a blade server?
questions.why: blade that plugs into a large chassis, built for redundancy and resilience - rack servers are mounted in a rack, usually 1 RU.

questions.source: Q1. A Windows PC shows IPv4 address 169.254.12.7. What happened?
questions.q: A Windows PC shows IPv4 address 169.254.12.7. What happened?
questions.why: It did not get an address from DHCP and used an automatic private (APIPA) address - check VLAN, DHCP server and relay.

questions.source: Q2. Which route print column shows the next-hop router for the default route?
questions.q: Which route print column shows the next-hop router for the default route?
questions.why: Gateway. The Interface column is the PC's own address.

questions.source: Q3. Which Linux command replaces ifconfig for showing addresses?
questions.q: Which Linux command replaces ifconfig for showing addresses?
questions.why: ip addr - ifconfig may not even be installed.

questions.source: Q4. What does the %11 after a Windows IPv6 link-local address mean?
questions.q: What does the %11 after a Windows IPv6 link-local address mean?
questions.why: The interface index (zone ID). It is not part of the address - you may need it when you ping a link-local address.

questions.source: Q1. Which of the four host tests first proves the cable and the local LAN work?
questions.q: Which of the four host tests first proves the cable and the local LAN work?
questions.why: Pinging the default gateway - pinging 127.0.0.1 or your own IP never leaves the host.

questions.source: Q2. PC1 can ping its gateway, but not a remote server. tracert stops after the first hop. Where do you look next?
questions.q: PC1 can ping its gateway, but not a remote server. tracert stops after the first hop. Where do you look next?
questions.why: On the gateway router: its routing table (and the return route), then ACLs - the host is already proven good.

questions.source: Q3. Ping to a server works but Telnet or HTTP fails. What is the likely cause?
questions.q: Ping to a server works but Telnet or HTTP fails. What is the likely cause?
questions.why: n ACL or firewall blocking the port, or the service is not running - ping uses ICMP only. Check show access-lists and show ip interface.

questions.source: Q4. A port shows many late collisions. What is the usual cause?
questions.q: A port shows many late collisions. What is the usual cause?
questions.why: duplex mismatch (the half-duplex side shows them) - check both ends: both auto or both fixed.

questions.source: Q5. Why could R2 telnet to Server1 even though ACL 110 blocked Telnet from PC1?
questions.q: Why could R2 telnet to Server1 even though ACL 110 blocked Telnet from PC1?
questions.why: CLs filter traffic passing through the router, not traffic the router originates - this is why you should test from the real source host.

questions.source: Q1. Why can a sniffer on a switch port not see other hosts' unicast traffic?
questions.q: Why can a sniffer on a switch port not see other hosts' unicast traffic?
questions.why: The switch forwards unicast frames only to the port where the destination MAC address is - a hub sent everything to every port.

questions.source: Q2. What does SPAN do?
questions.q: What does SPAN do?
questions.why: opies traffic from source port(s) to a destination port where an analyser is connected - the original traffic is not changed.

questions.source: Q3. Which command verifies a SPAN session in the book?
questions.q: Which command verifies a SPAN session in the book?
questions.why: show monitor (show monitor session 1 on current IOS) - the longer form is the common modern syntax. CHECK

questions.source: Q1. Why does the Block_Telnet ACL end with permit ip any any?
questions.q: Why does the Block_Telnet ACL end with permit ip any any?
questions.why: Without it the implicit deny at the end would block all other traffic - every ACL has an implicit deny ip any any.

questions.source: Q2. Where should an extended ACL be placed?
questions.q: Where should an extended ACL be placed?
questions.why: losest to the source of the traffic - a standard ACL goes closest to the destination.

questions.source: Q3. How do you remove line 10 of a named ACL and add a corrected line 10?
questions.q: How do you remove line 10 of a named ACL and add a corrected line 10?
questions.why: In ACL configuration mode: no 10, then 10 deny ... - you do not need to retype the whole ACL.

questions.source: Q4. Write the ACL address and wildcard for the subnet 192.168.10.64/26.
questions.q: Write the ACL address and wildcard for the subnet 192.168.10.64/26.
questions.why: 192.168.10.64 0.0.0.63 - usable hosts are .65 to .126. Calculated by script.

questions.source: Q1. Which IPv6 address does a host normally use as its default gateway?
questions.q: Which IPv6 address does a host normally use as its default gateway?
questions.why: The router interface's link-local address, learned from a router advertisement - not the global address.

questions.source: Q2. You add an IPv6 static route with a link-local next hop but no exit interface. What happens?
questions.q: You add an IPv6 static route with a link-local next hop but no exit interface. What happens?
questions.why: IOS rejects it. A link-local next hop requires the exit interface - the same fe80 address could exist on every link.

questions.source: Q3. Which command shows the IPv6 equivalent of the ARP cache on a Cisco router?
questions.q: Which command shows the IPv6 equivalent of the ARP cache on a Cisco router?
questions.why: show ipv6 neighbors - on Windows use netsh interface ipv6 show neighbor.

questions.source: Q4. Hosts never learn an IPv6 default gateway, though the router interface is up. Name one likely cause.
questions.q: Hosts never learn an IPv6 default gateway, though the router interface is up. Name one likely cause.
questions.why: ipv6 unicast-routing is not enabled on the router, so it sends no router advertisements - RA guard or an ACL could also block RAs.

questions.source: Q1. Which multicast address does a host send a router solicitation to?
questions.q: Which multicast address does a host send a router solicitation to?
questions.why: FF02::2 (all routers). Routers answer with an RA.

questions.source: Q2. What is the solicited-node multicast address of a host whose address ends in ...:3ab7, with last 24 bits 11:3ab7?
questions.q: What is the solicited-node multicast address of a host whose address ends in ...:3ab7, with last 24 bits 11:3ab7?
questions.why: FF02::1:FF11:3AB7 - FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits.

questions.source: Q3. An IPv6 neighbour entry is STALE. A packet is now sent to that neighbour. What state comes next?
questions.q: An IPv6 neighbour entry is STALE. A packet is now sent to that neighbour. What state comes next?
questions.why: ELAY, then PROBE if no confirmation arrives - if the neighbour confirms, it returns to REACH.

questions.source: Q1. A port shows Access Mode VLAN: 20 (Inactive). What do you check first?
questions.q: A port shows Access Mode VLAN: 20 (Inactive). What do you check first?
questions.why: Whether VLAN 20 exists on this switch (show vlan brief). Create it if it is missing - an inactive VLAN means the database lacks it.

questions.source: Q2. Why does a host not appear in the MAC address table?
questions.q: Why does a host not appear in the MAC address table?
questions.why: Its port is down, in an inactive VLAN, or the host is silent. Check port state and VLAN - the switch learns MACs from received frames.

questions.source: Q3. Which command shows the access VLAN, native VLAN and operational mode of one port?
questions.q: Which command shows the access VLAN, native VLAN and operational mode of one port?
questions.why: show interfaces <int> switchport - show vlan does not show trunk ports.

questions.source: Q1. Which command shows the DTP status of an interface?
questions.q: Which command shows the DTP status of an interface?
questions.why: show dtp interface <int>.

questions.source: Q2. Which two commands help you spot a native VLAN mismatch?
questions.q: Which two commands help you spot a native VLAN mismatch?
questions.why: show interfaces trunk and show interfaces <int> switchport - compare the native VLAN on both switches.

questions.source: Q3. Which port mode generates no DTP frames?
questions.q: Which port mode generates no DTP frames?
questions.why: Nonegotiate. It is allowed only when the port is manually set to trunk or access.

questions.source: Q4. Two new switches are cabled together and both ports are at the default. They did not trunk. Why?
questions.q: Two new switches are cabled together and both ports are at the default. They did not trunk. Why?
questions.why: oth ports are dynamic auto; neither end asks for a trunk - set one end to desirable or trunk.

questions.source: Q1. List the four host ping tests in order and say what each one proves.
questions.q: List the four host ping tests in order and say what each one proves.
